title: Israel Hit Iran's Petrochemical Lifeline. For India, It Means $97 Oil and No End in Sight.
excerpt: The first strike on Iranian energy infrastructure since the April ceasefire sends Brent surging, the IRGC retaliating on Haifa, and the Strait of Hormuz further from reopening.
body:
Israel struck the Mahshahr petrochemical complex in Iran's southwest on Monday — the first hit on an Iranian energy site since the April 8 ceasefire — and within hours, the global oil market delivered its verdict. Brent crude surged past $97 a barrel, erasing Friday's hopes of de-escalation and dragging India's import calculus deeper into crisis territory.

The Israeli military confirmed targeting multiple facilities at Mahshahr, one of Iran's largest petrochemical hubs. A provincial official told Iran's semi-official Fars news agency that parts of the plant were damaged. Authorities ordered all employees to evacuate, though no injuries were reported. Five production lines at the complex have now been hit since the wider war began on February 28.

Israel also launched what it described as a large-scale strike on Iranian defence systems to dismantle air defence capabilities that Tehran had been deploying. Explosions were reported in Tehran, with Iran's Mehr news agency claiming air defences shot down a drone over the capital.

## The Retaliation Cycle

The IRGC responded by launching a missile attack on a "similar plant" in the Israeli city of Haifa. It also fired 11 ballistic missiles at Israeli targets, according to Israel's ambassador to Washington, Yechiel Leiter. Israel said its defence systems intercepted the incoming missiles.

Yemen's Houthi militia, aligned with Iran, pledged to halt Israel's maritime navigation in the Red Sea and claimed responsibility for the first missile attack on Israel since the ceasefire — a move that further complicates the already-paralysed shipping lanes that once carried a fifth of the world's crude oil and LNG.

The escalation came despite a reported phone call between U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday. According to Axios, Trump urged Netanyahu to refrain from further strikes because "we are close to doing something good in terms of a deal."

Trump, speaking to the Financial Times, was characteristically blunt: "It's not going to have any impact on the deal. I call the shots. I call all the shots. He doesn't call the shots."

## What $97 Oil Means for India

India imports roughly 85 per cent of its crude oil. Every sustained $10 increase in the Brent benchmark adds an estimated $15 billion to the country's annual import bill. At $97, Brent has climbed nearly 60 per cent since the start of the Iran war, though it remains below the $120 peak reached in March.

The immediate damage was visible across Indian markets on Monday. The rupee fell 0.8 per cent to 95.7075 per dollar — its sharpest single-session drop in four weeks — reversing nearly all of Friday's rally that had followed the RBI's emergency capital inflows package. The Nifty 50 dropped 1.04 per cent to 23,123, closing at a two-month low.

"The crude spike brought external risks back into focus for the rupee, given India's heavy dependence on imports and the currency's sensitivity to swings in energy prices," Reuters reported. Higher oil prices widen India's import bill, pressure the current account, and increase demand for dollars from oil marketing companies — a triple blow to an economy that was already battling record foreign portfolio outflows.

## The Hormuz Question

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world's oil and LNG once flowed, has been effectively blockaded since the war began. Iran controls the northern shore; Washington has imposed its own blockade on Iranian ports from the south. While both sides have signalled they are close to a preliminary deal to reopen the strait, the Mahshahr strike makes that timeline murkier.

Iran's chief peace negotiator, Parliamentary Speaker Mohammed Baqer Qalibaf, said U.S. bases and Israeli assets were "legitimate targets" because of hostile acts, including what he called the "violation of agreements over Lebanon." Tehran has long demanded that any peace deal with Washington include a ceasefire in Lebanon, which Israel invaded in March and has continued to strike despite a U.S.-brokered truce announced last week.

For India, the strategic calculus is simple but punishing: diversify supply chains, absorb the cost, and wait for a deal that keeps slipping. The government has already pivoted to sourcing oil from Latin America, Africa, and new suppliers, but none of those routes match the volume or pricing that the Hormuz corridor once offered.

Monday's strike was a reminder that in this war, every escalation has an Indian price tag.

*Sources: Reuters, OilPrice.com, Financial Times, Inshorts*
